mappings.note: Argues why groundwater must be conserved (C-SCI4.1, since LO-94 lists only pollutants, trees and sanitation) and names a cause of its depletion (LO-85, whose own example is the water table falling through human activity).
Ice stupas explained as artificial glaciers that bank winter water for the growing season: conservation of a scarce resource.
Hollow bricks moderating a house in both seasons: trapped air used in building, an everyday application.
Compares conduction and convection on particle movement and medium, a contrast between two modes of transfer.
Describes the wax-and-pins experiment and its observations (LO-84) and then draws the conduction conclusion from them (LO-86).
The potassium permanganate demonstration (LO-84) plus why convection matters in fluids (LO-86). Both are required by the question.
Sea and land breeze as convection cycles (LO-86), driven by land and water heating at different rates (LO-85, the cause the question asks to be explained).
All three modes defined with an example each and whether a medium is needed: the core mode-of-transfer item.
The water cycle in full, from the Sun's heat through evaporation and transpiration to condensation and precipitation: one long process explanation.
How groundwater forms and what an aquifer is (LO-86), then depletion and a way to recharge it (C-SCI4.1, resource conservation).
Why summer and winter clothing differ, argued from reflection, absorption and insulation: heat transfer applied to what we wear.
Compares how fast soil and water heat and cool (LO-82) and then uses that to explain the moderate coastal climate (LO-85).
Locates conduction, convection and radiation in a single bukhari heating a room and cooking food: the three modes identified in one setting.
Explains the ice stupa as water conservation for a dry region (C-SCI4.1) and ties it to the water cycle and climate of Ladakh (LO-86).
Paved cities cut infiltration, so aquifers are not recharged and levels fall: the water-table-and-human-activity cause named in LO-85.
Ceramic against steel for holding heat, and plastic handles against metal bodies: materials separated by how well they conduct.
Sand heats and cools faster than sea water, which is why the water feels warmer at night: two materials compared on their thermal behaviour.
Warmth from the fire falls off with distance because radiation weakens as it spreads: the felt effect traced to its cause.
Trapped air keeping a house or body warm is the everyday application (LO-93), and naming which transfer it cuts down calls on the modes themselves (LO-86).
